topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to dental education context — findings may not generalise to other healthcare professions or non-clinical fields, though the competency framework methodology could be adapted across disciplines.
takeaways: Use competency frameworks as a structured approach to embedding AI literacy into professional curricula — map technical skills, ethical reasoning, and practical application rather than treating AI as a standalone topic.
Identify domain-specific AI competencies (e.g., diagnostic imaging, treatment planning) relevant to your field before designing training programs, rather than adopting generic AI literacy modules.

articles.title: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce - U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.snippet: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce  U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes US Department of Labor initiatives, funding programmes, and policy frameworks that do not apply in Australia. May offer conceptual insights into workforce AI literacy strategy, but specific grants, schemes, and regulatory context are not transferable.
takeaways: Identifies that government-led AI literacy initiatives are being scaled at national level in the US; consider whether similar advocacy or funding mechanisms exist through Australian agencies (e.g. Department of Employment & Workplace Relations) or sector bodies.

Highlights the focus on workforce-wide AI capability as a policy priority; this suggests timing is right for Australian organisations to embed AI literacy into learning & development strategies before skills gaps widen.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to higher vocational education settings and may have limited application to workplace or general adult populations. Geographic scope and sample size not evident from title/snippet.
takeaways: A competency-based ladder pathway can structure AI literacy development in stages — consider adopting a similar tiered progression model when designing AI training for your workforce, starting with foundational concepts before advancing to applied skills.

Competency frameworks validated in educational settings may require adaptation for workplace contexts — pilot test any vocational education model with your employee population to ensure relevance to job roles and organisational goals.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely moderate — focuses on higher education sector which has distinct characteristics; applicability to workplace AI literacy development depends on how directly strategies translate from academic to organisational settings.
takeaways: Higher education institutions are developing structured curricula and competency frameworks for AI — identify which of these frameworks (e.g., technical foundations, ethical reasoning, domain application) are most relevant to reskill your workforce.

Academic AI literacy strategies often emphasise hands-on project-based learning and interdisciplinary approaches — consider embedding similar practices (cross-functional projects, practical tooling) into your employee development programs rather than relying solely on theoretical training.

articles.title: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation - Nature
articles.snippet: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone — geographic scope, sample size, sector coverage, and methodology are not disclosed. The focus on 'employability skills' suggests applicability across sectors, but this requires confirmation from the full article.
takeaways: Employability skills — likely including AI literacy, adaptability, and collaboration — appear to be key drivers of job quality in AI-transformed roles; prioritise upskilling programs that develop these competencies alongside technical AI knowledge.

Academic achievement and intrinsic motivation both influence how effectively employability skills translate into quality employment outcomes; consider motivational factors (e.g. career development pathways, autonomy) alongside capability-building when designing AI literacy interventions.

articles.title: New AI Course from DOL Targets Broad Workforce Readiness - SHRM
articles.snippet: New AI Course from DOL Targets Broad Workforce Readiness  SHRM
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes a US Department of Labor initiative and program that would not directly transfer to Australian workforce development contexts or funding structures.
takeaways: US-specific: The DOL course represents a government-funded approach to AI literacy; Australian organisations should explore equivalent programs through state and federal training bodies or design internal courses aligned with local competency frameworks.

Broad workforce readiness in AI suggests targeting multiple skill levels and job functions rather than technical roles only — consider mapping which roles in your organisation need foundational AI literacy versus advanced capabilities.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. Without access to methodology section, ability to assess geographic scope, sample size, and sector coverage is limited.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger either approach (skill-building, role expansion) or avoidance (task withdrawal, disengagement) job crafting behaviours — understanding which employees gravitate toward each response helps tailor upskilling and change management strategies.

Approach-avoidance framing suggests employees' psychological orientation toward AI may be as important as the technology itself; screening for risk tolerance and growth mindset during AI rollout could identify who needs additional support versus mentoring opportunities.

Job crafting offers a measurable lens for monitoring how AI adoption is affecting employee agency and motivation — tracking these behavioural shifts can provide early warning signs of adoption resistance or burnout.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to organisations with paternalistic leadership models; generalisability to Western flat or matrix-structured organisations may be limited. Geographic scope and sample size not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in AI customisation and configuration decisions — this strengthens collaboration and engagement with AI systems.
Paternalistic leaders can leverage their mentoring relationships to guide employees toward viewing AI as a resource to craft and shape, rather than a tool imposed upon them.
Create structured opportunities for 'AI crafting' (tailoring AI outputs and workflows to individual or team needs) as a mechanism to bridge the gap between employee buy-in and effective AI adoption.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual argument rather than empirical evidence. Likely draws on diverse international examples but lacks specific sample details or rigorous research methodology.
takeaways: Prioritise AI augmentation (enhancing human capability) over full automation to preserve employee engagement, skill development, and institutional knowledge—particularly valuable for roles requiring judgment and client relationships.

Design AI implementations that position technology as a tool for upskilling rather than replacement; this approach can improve retention, reduce change resistance, and build competitive advantage through a more capable workforce.

Conduct a skills audit before AI deployment to identify which tasks should be augmented (human + AI) versus automated, ensuring decisions align with long-term organisational culture and talent strategy.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to the full article; the snippet does not provide sufficient methodological detail regarding sample size, geography, sector, or study design.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical buffer against negative mental health outcomes during AI adoption — prioritise creating an environment where employees feel safe to voice concerns, ask questions, and admit mistakes when working with new AI tools.

Before or during AI implementation, assess baseline psychological safety in your teams; low psychological safety suggests you need deliberate interventions (e.g. leader modelling vulnerability, normalising failure, clear escalation paths) before rolling out AI to minimise depression and disengagement risk.
Use this finding to make a business case for investing in psychological safety practices alongside AI upskilling — framing it as both a wellbeing imperative and a productivity safeguard.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on sample size, sector, and geographic scope not evident from title/snippet. The moderating role of self-efficacy and transformational leadership may vary across different organisational contexts and cultures.
takeaways: Leaders can mitigate AI-driven job insecurity by adopting transformational leadership practices that inspire confidence and provide clear vision during technological transitions.
Invest in building employee self-efficacy around AI tools through training and skill development — this appears to buffer against anxiety about job displacement.
When implementing AI, explicitly address job insecurity concerns and ensure leaders communicate how roles will evolve rather than disappear, supported by visible upskilling opportunities.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to synthesise existing research on AI and workforce development, but geographic scope and specific sectors covered are unclear from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Co-skilling programmes (pairing AI training with role-specific skills) are more effective than standalone upskilling at reducing job insecurity and engagement loss when AI is introduced.

Organisational support structures — including transparent communication about AI implementation, career pathways, and psychological safety — directly moderate the relationship between AI adoption and employee anxiety.
Proactive job insecurity mitigation during AI transitions requires early involvement of affected staff in implementation planning, not just post-deployment communication.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) is broadly applicable across sectors and geographies, but empirical findings may be limited by the specific organizational contexts studied.
takeaways: Monitor whether employees respond to AI adoption by either proactively reshaping their roles (approach-oriented job crafting) or withdrawing from tasks (avoidance-oriented job crafting); tailor change management to encourage the former by highlighting skill development and role clarity.

Design AI implementation to explicitly address psychological safety and perceived control — employees who feel threatened by AI are more likely to avoid or resist, whereas those who see AI as augmenting their capabilities are more likely to actively craft their jobs to leverage it.

Track job crafting behavior changes during AI rollouts as an early indicator of adoption success; significant uptick in avoidance behaviors signals need for additional training, communication, or role redesign support.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Insights may reflect US higher education and business perspectives primarily.
takeaways: Clarify with your team which specific work processes AI will reshape in your organisation rather than assuming broad disruption — targeted change management works better than organisation-wide anxiety responses.
Identify early adopters within your workforce who can model AI-enabled workflows for others; peer-led behaviour change typically outperforms top-down mandates when introducing new tools.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on global client experience and research, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic focus are unclear from the snippet provided. Findings may reflect practices in large, digitally mature organisations.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation—prioritise upskilling and role redesign alongside tools and systems.
Design behaviour change interventions that address how employees' roles, responsibilities, and career pathways will shift, not just what new systems they'll use.
Build internal communication and change management around the interdependence of AI tools and human capability development to increase adoption and reduce resistance.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a strategic perspective on AI implementation approaches but lacks empirical data or case studies to support claims about long-run competitive outcomes. Applicability may vary by industry, organisation size, and workforce composition.
takeaways: When designing AI rollouts, prioritise augmentation (AI enhancing human capabilities) over full automation to preserve workforce engagement and institutional knowledge—this can reduce resistance to change and maintain employee morale during transition.
Frame AI adoption conversations with teams around skill development and role enhancement rather than job displacement; this reframing supports psychological safety and encourages uptake of new tools.

articles.title: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet. The theoretical framework (conservation of resources theory) is well-established, but geographic scope, sector representation, and sample size are unclear from the provided information.
takeaways: Employee attitudes toward AI ('liking of AI') act as a critical moderator — organisations should invest in building positive perceptions of generative AI tools before rolling them out, not just focusing on technical training.

Job crafting emerges as a mechanism linking AI adoption to outcomes — encourage employees to actively reshape their tasks and responsibilities in response to AI capabilities rather than passively accepting new workflows.

Monitor career commitment during AI transitions; if employees perceive AI as a threat rather than a resource, they may disengage from long-term career growth — frame AI adoption as a career development opportunity, not a replacement threat.

articles.title: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work across sectors and geographies, but specific organisational contexts and implementation details may vary; findings skew towards large enterprises with resources for major transformation.
takeaways: Map how gen AI will reconfigure specific roles and workflows in your organisation before rolling out change initiatives — this allows you to design targeted upskilling and redeployment strategies rather than generic training.

Embed change management from the outset of AI implementation, not as an afterthought — clarity on what's changing, why, and how employees fit into the new model reduces resistance and speeds adoption.
Communicate how gen AI complements (not replaces) employee skills; frame adoption around augmentation and efficiency gains to build buy-in and psychological safety around the technology.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report summarising research findings without details on sample size, methodology, or geographic scope. Actual generalisability depends on the underlying study, which is not described in the snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging has detected structural or functional differences in the brains of individuals with psychopathic traits — a finding that challenges the idea that psychopathy is purely behavioural or a choice.

The discovery is striking because it suggests neurobiology may underlie traits like reduced empathy or emotional processing, making psychopathy a measurable neurological condition rather than just a personality type.

This kind of research fascinates people because it bridges neuroscience and pop-culture fascination with psychopathy, raising the tantalising question: if the brain is 'wired' differently, how much can behaviour be controlled or changed?

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — methodology, sample size, and geographic scope not detailed. Generalisability depends on the wine review dataset analysed (likely English-language reviews from online platforms) and whether findings hold across different cultures and wine-consuming populations.
takeaways: AI can infer personality traits from seemingly trivial writing like wine reviews — suggesting that how we describe our everyday experiences (not just formal assessments) reveals something genuine about who we are.

The 'wine personality link' is a delightful example of how machine learning finds hidden patterns in human behaviour that we'd never spot manually, and a good reminder that AI can uncover surprising connections in places we'd least expect them.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline news report with insufficient methodological detail to assess study scope, sample size, or geographic location. The underlying research may have varying applicability depending on whether it was a clinical sample, population study, or specific country.
takeaways: A unexpected biological link emerged: people with hyperthyroidism showed associations with dark personality traits like narcissism or callousness — a finding that challenges our understanding of how thyroid dysfunction affects personality and behaviour.

The result is intriguing because it suggests personality variation might have a physiological basis beyond psychology alone, hinting that hormonal imbalances could influence how people relate to others in ways we don't normally think about.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the underlying sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet provided. Without knowing the geographic scope, sample size, and demographic representation, it is difficult to assess how broadly these findings apply across cultures and populations.
takeaways: The Big Five personality model can be subdivided into ten more granular aspects, revealing nuances in gender differences that the standard five-factor model might miss — a finding that challenges the assumption that broad personality categories tell the whole story.

Gender differences in personality aren't uniform across all traits; some aspects show larger gaps than others, suggesting that sweeping generalisations about 'how men and women differ' are oversimplified and worth scrutinising.

This research hints at why gender stereotypes persist despite psychological reality being more complicated — we tend to notice the differences that stand out while overlooking traits where genders overlap significantly.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited without seeing the full article — twin studies typically assume equal environments and shared genetics, which may not fully capture environmental and social influences on political beliefs. Generalisability depends on the sample's geographic origin and demographic composition.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian political beliefs have a heritable component, suggesting nature and nurture both shape political ideology in unexpected ways.
The finding is counterintuitive because it challenges the common assumption that political beliefs are purely learned or chosen — genetics appears to play a measurable role.
It's a reminder that deeply held convictions about governance and authority have biological roots, making political polarisation a more complex human phenomenon than ideology alone.

articles.title: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age - Nature
articles.snippet: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition — findings may be specific to the age groups and populations tested, though publication in Nature suggests rigorous methodology.
takeaways: Curiosity and surprise don't boost memory the same way across all ages — your brain's learning tricks change as you get older, which is counterintuitive given we often assume memory aids work universally.
The finding that these emotional states have age-dependent effects on memory challenges one-size-fits-all approaches to education and information design.
This suggests why a surprising fact might stick with a 20-year-old differently than a 60-year-old — their brains are literally wired to encode novelty in different ways.

topics.label: Psychological Safety

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on academic settings with multicultural teams. Findings may not generalise to corporate or non-academic organisational contexts. Sample characteristics and size unclear from snippet.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to prompt leaders toward more inclusive decision-making in diverse teams, but effectiveness depends on how algorithms are built and whether leaders actively engage with the prompts rather than override them.

In teams with gender imbalances, relying solely on AI-assisted leadership without addressing underlying cultural or structural barriers may create an illusion of inclusion without shifting actual outcomes for underrepresented groups.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad global reach, but findings depend on PwC's sampling methodology and respondent demographics (typically skews toward white-collar, professional workers in developed economies). Specific regional variations may not be fully representative of all workforce segments.
takeaways: Identify which psychological safety concerns (e.g., job security, workplace relationships, speaking up) rank highest among your workforce by comparing your organisation's culture against PwC's global benchmarks.

Use the survey's hope and fear themes to shape listening sessions or pulse surveys within your own organisation — tailor safety initiatives to address the specific anxieties your teams are experiencing rather than assuming global patterns apply uniformly.

Monitor whether psychological safety gaps correlate with the hopes/fears identified in the survey to understand if unaddressed workforce concerns are eroding trust and willingness to contribute ideas.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident in title/snippet. The mechanism proposed (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) may vary by organisational context, leadership quality, and implementation approach. Findings likely most relevant to organisations with rapid, poorly-managed AI rollouts.
takeaways: AI adoption alone doesn't cause employee depression — the pathway runs through psychological safety. Leaders must actively protect employees' ability to speak up about AI concerns, ask questions, and report problems without fear of judgment or retaliation during implementation.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor. Model transparent decision-making about AI use, acknowledge legitimate concerns employees raise, and demonstrate that you're prioritising worker wellbeing alongside productivity gains.

Monitor psychological safety metrics before, during, and after AI adoption. If safety scores drop, investigate whether employees feel safe voicing concerns about automation, skill gaps, or job security — and address these directly rather than assuming depression stems from the technology itself.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Likely draws on BCG's global consulting experience, but specific geographic scope and sample composition are unclear from the snippet. Findings may be most applicable to large, multinational organisations BCG typically works with.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that welcome diverse perspectives and dissent — frame disagreement as valuable input rather than disloyalty, particularly for underrepresented groups who may self-silence in low-safety environments.
Measure psychological safety systematically through employee surveys and focus groups, then tie accountability to leaders' safety-building behaviours in performance reviews to move beyond rhetoric.

Address power dynamics directly: train managers to solicit quiet voices, acknowledge their own fallibility, and visibly respond to concerns raised — small, visible changes signal safety more than grand statements.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on general workplace dynamics and assumed employee behaviour patterns, but lacks empirical data on scope or geography. Findings likely most relevant to knowledge-worker settings in Western organisations.
takeaways: Create explicit psychological safety around AI tool use by separating experimentation from performance evaluation — employees hide AI usage when they fear it signals incompetence or job security concerns.

Establish clear, published guidelines on approved AI tools and use cases to reduce the ambiguity that drives employees to operate in shadow — transparent policies reduce perceived risk of using AI openly.
Build trust through leader modelling: when managers visibly discuss their own AI experiments and learning, it signals that transparency is safer than concealment and normalises AI as part of work.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual clarifications about psychological safety but lacks empirical data on geographic or sectoral applicability. The Harvard affiliation suggests US context, though the core misconceptions about psychological safety likely apply across cultures.
takeaways: Identify and challenge common myths about psychological safety in your organisation — misconceptions may be preventing you from implementing evidence-based approaches that actually work.
Use this resource to educate leaders and teams on what psychological safety actually is and isn't, which can shift conversations away from ineffective or contradictory initiatives.
Recognise that debunking false beliefs about psychological safety is a necessary first step before rolling out interventions, as misconceptions can undermine buy-in and effectiveness.
